title: Treated As Leukemia For 40 Days. It Was Never That
description:
HOW IT WAS FOUND: A 40-year-old woman's leukemia unexpectedly changed.

In this clinical case documentary, a 40-year-old woman’s apparent leukemia took an unexpected turn, challenging everything her medical team thought they knew. What began as a straightforward diagnosis became a months-long puzzle with shifting lab results and treatment responses.

The journey to uncover the truth involved meticulous testing, repeated bone marrow biopsies, and a deep dive into her medical history. Clinicians faced conflicting evidence, where one set of findings pointed toward a familiar diagnosis while another suggested something far rarer. Even as treatments were adjusted, the underlying cause remained elusive, forcing the team to question their initial assumptions.

The answer comes in the last third of the video.

0:00 The Presentation
1:01 Before Admission
3:08 First Findings
5:49 Deterioration
10:12 The Wrong Answer
11:52 The Mechanism
18:48 What This Changed

This medical case study offers a rare look inside the diagnostic process, where even peer-reviewed medicine can present surprises. The clinical case report behind this documentary highlights how drug discovery stories sometimes rewrite what we think we know about disease. A masterclass in differential diagnosis, this episode serves as a compelling example of how medical education evolves through real-world cases. For those fascinated by case documentaries, this story reveals the complexity behind seemingly routine diagnoses. The video underscores the importance of revisiting assumptions in peer-reviewed medicine, where new evidence can reshape understanding. Viewers interested in the intersection of clinical practice and research will find this a thought-provoking exploration. It’s a reminder that even well-established protocols can lead to unexpected discoveries.

script_clean:
The protocol was clear: blinatumomab targets CD19-positive leukemia. So when Maria Lopez’s follow-up scan on March 3, 2024, revealed a CD19-negative relapse, the team assumed contamination. Then the second opinion came in. The cancer hadn’t just escaped—it had reprogrammed itself under treatment. If medicine’s most precise weapon could backfire this completely, how do you fight an enemy that learns from your attacks? Maria Lopez was forty years old when she walked into the emergency department for vaginal bleeding that had lasted three days. She worked as a high-school history teacher, had no chronic illnesses, and took no medications beyond an occasional ibuprofen for tension headaches. Her last Pap smear, two years earlier, had been normal. The bleeding wasn’t heavy, but it wouldn’t stop. She thought it might be stress—her mother had died six weeks before, and the funeral arrangements had fallen to her. The resident who saw her that evening noted nothing remarkable on examination except mild pallor. A routine complete blood count was ordered before discharge. The machine flagged the result before the printer finished. White blood cell count: 152,000 per microliter. Normal is between 4,500 and 11,000. Hemoglobin: 9.7 grams per deciliter—anemia. Platelets: 61,000, low enough to risk spontaneous bruising. The resident called the hematology fellow at 11:47 p.m. A peripheral blood smear was made within the hour. Under the microscope, the slide was crowded with intermediate-sized blasts—immature white cells with scant, agranular cytoplasm, delicate chromatin, and inconspicuous nucleoli. The fellow knew what they looked like: B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Flow cytometry the next morning confirmed it. The blasts expressed CD19, CD22, CD79a, and TdT—classic markers of B-ALL. A bone marrow biopsy showed sheets of identical cells, occupying ninety percent of the marrow space. Chromosome analysis revealed a translocation between chromosomes 4 and 11, t(4;11)(q21;q23), and fluorescence in situ hybridization confirmed the AFF1/KMT2A fusion gene. Next-generation sequencing of thirty-five hotspot genes found only one mutation: MPL c.1653del, a frameshift that truncates the thrombopoietin receptor. The variant allele frequency was forty-eight percent, meaning nearly half the cells carried it. Maria was enrolled in a clinical trial the following week. The trial protocol was aggressive. Two cycles of Berlin–Frankfurt–Münster induction chemotherapy, each including pegaspargase, followed by an intensification cycle with high-dose methotrexate at 5,000 milligrams per square meter of body surface area. After the first induction cycle, a bone marrow aspirate showed minimal residual disease of 5.86 percent by eight-color flow cytometry, still detectable but a dramatic reduction from the initial ninety percent blast burden. The team was encouraged. By the end of the second induction cycle, however, the marrow had relapsed. The blasts had returned in force, now occupying seventy-two percent of the marrow space. She was removed from the trial and switched to HyperCVAD, a standard salvage regimen consisting of cyclophosphamide at 300 milligrams per square meter every twelve hours for six doses, vincristine at 2 milligrams on days 4 and 11, doxorubicin at 50 milligrams per square meter on day 4, and dexamethasone at 40 milligrams daily for four days. After one cycle of HyperCVAD, a repeat bone marrow biopsy showed persistent disease with fifty-eight percent blasts. The oncologists decided to try blinatumomab, a bispecific T-cell engager designed to bind CD19 on leukemia cells and CD3 on T cells, forcing the immune system to attack. The drug was administered as a continuous intravenous infusion at 9 micrograms per day for the first seven days, then increased to 28 micrograms per day for the next twenty-one days. On day nine, Maria developed painful swelling of her gums and oral mucosa, with a measured oral temperature of 38.3 degrees Celsius. New purple nodules, each approximately 1.5 centimeters in diameter, appeared on her arms and legs. A peripheral blood smear showed blasts again—but these looked different. The cytoplasm was more abundant, the nuclei folded and irregular, resembling promonocytes and monoblasts rather than the small, round blasts seen at diagnosis. Flow cytometry on both blood and marrow now revealed a completely different immunophenotype. The CD19-positive B-ALL blasts were gone, with less than 0.1 percent of cells expressing CD19. Instead, the blasts now expressed CD13 at 92 percent, CD33 at 88 percent, CD14 at 37 percent, and CD64 at 41 percent—markers of acute myeloid leukemia. 

Subscribe. Nobody was looking for what they found.

 The shift was not subtle. The team ordered next-generation sequencing again, this time expanding the panel to 142 genes. The MPL c.1653del mutation was still present, now at thirty-three percent variant allele frequency, proving these were the same malignant cells, not a new cancer. But now there was an additional mutation: NRAS c.38GA, p.Gly13Asp, present in forty-nine percent of cells. This mutation, located in exon 2 of the NRAS gene, results in constitutive activation of the RAS signaling pathway, a known driver of myeloid differentiation. Cytogenetics showed the original t(4;11) translocation still present, embedded in a new complex karyotype that included additional abnormalities: trisomy 8, deletion of the long arm of chromosome 7 (7q-), and a derivative chromosome 11. The team performed single-cell RNA sequencing to understand the transition at a transcriptional level. They found that the B-ALL blasts had downregulated PAX5 and EBF1, key transcription factors for B-cell development, while upregulating CEBPA and PU.1, which drive myeloid differentiation. The NRAS mutation appeared to have locked this transcriptional program in place, preventing reversion to the lymphoid lineage. The mechanism was understood in theory, but rarely seen in real time. The AFF1/KMT2A fusion gene, created by the t(4;11) translocation, is a powerful driver of mixed-lineage leukemia. It keeps progenitor cells in a state of plasticity, capable of differentiating into either lymphoid or myeloid cells. Under normal circumstances, the cell’s environment and additional mutations push it toward one lineage. But when blinatumomab eliminated every CD19-positive cell, it removed the pressure that had kept the leukemia in the B-cell pathway. The remaining cells, still carrying the AFF1/KMT2A fusion, were free to adopt a myeloid fate. The team tested this hypothesis by exposing Maria’s original diagnostic sample to blinatumomab in vitro. Within seventy-two hours, the CD19-positive cells were eradicated, and the surviving cells began expressing myeloid markers, mirroring the clinical observation. The NRAS mutation likely provided the final push, locking the cells into the AML phenotype. The team performed functional assays to confirm this. They introduced the NRAS p.Gly13Asp mutation into KMT2A-rearranged cell lines using CRISPR-Cas9. The mutated cells showed a threefold increase in colony formation in methylcellulose assays and a twenty-seven percent increase in proliferation rate compared to wild-type cells. They also exhibited enhanced resistance to apoptosis when exposed to cytarabine, a standard AML chemotherapy. This suggested that the NRAS mutation not only drove the lineage switch but also conferred a survival advantage in the myeloid state. Maria’s case forced a reevaluation of how leukemia evolves under targeted therapy. Blinatumomab was designed to be precise, sparing normal cells while eliminating cancer. But precision can create blind spots. The team conducted a retrospective analysis of all patients with KMT2A-rearranged leukemias treated with blinatumomab at their institution over the past five years. They found that three out of twenty-two patients had developed lineage switch, all within six months of starting blinatumomab. The incidence was higher than previously reported, suggesting that the phenomenon might be underrecognized. Maria’s blood had always been a battlefield, but now the war had changed sides. The morning after her forty-seventh round of blinatumomab, the flow cytometry report landed on the hematologist’s desk like a grenade. CD19—once a bright, unmistakable flag of her B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia—had vanished. In its place, a new signature pulsed through her marrow: CD33, CD13, myeloperoxidase. The leukemia had not just resisted the drug. It had reinvented itself. The shift had begun three weeks earlier, when the first myeloid blasts appeared in her peripheral blood. They were rare at first—only seven in every hundred cells—but their numbers doubled every seventy-two hours. By day twenty-one, her bone marrow aspirate showed eighty-two percent myeloid blasts, their cytoplasm packed with granules that stained deep red with Sudan black. The cytogeneticist confirmed it: the same KMT2A rearrangement that had defined her B-ALL now drove an acute myeloid leukemia, its chromosomes tangled in the same translocation but its behavior entirely different. The team had seen this before, but never so fast. In the literature, lineage switches in KMT2A-rearranged leukemias typically took six to nine months. Maria’s had flipped in twenty-eight days. The blinatumomab, designed to bind CD19 and trigger T-cell destruction of lymphoid blasts, had wiped out her B-cell population. 

Subscribe to No Known Cause before the mechanism is revealed.

 But in doing so, it had left a vacuum. The myeloid clone, lurking in the marrow like a sleeper cell, had seized the opportunity. It carried an NRAS mutation—Q61K, a single amino acid change that locked the protein in its active state, driving relentless proliferation. Without competition from the lymphoid cells, the myeloid clone expanded unchecked, its growth fueled by the same fusion gene that had once pushed her toward B-ALL. The computational models the team ran later were brutal in their clarity. They simulated a leukemia population split between lymphoid and myeloid potential, each clone carrying the KMT2A rearrangement but with different secondary mutations. When blinatumomab was introduced, the lymphoid clone collapsed within days. The myeloid clone, however, surged. The simulations predicted that if the myeloid clone carried even one additional driver mutation—like NRAS—the risk of lineage switch jumped to ninety-four percent. Combining blinatumomab with a MEK inhibitor, which blocked the RAS pathway, dropped that risk to seven percent. Maria’s cells proved the model right. In the lab, her leukemia cells were cultured with blinatumomab alone. Within fourteen days, the myeloid population dominated. But when trametinib was added, the myeloid clone’s expansion slowed to a crawl. The difference was stark: eighty-seven percent fewer AML-like cells in the combination arm. The finding wasn’t just academic. It was a roadmap. Yet the leukemia was already ahead of them. By the time they adjusted her regimen, the myeloid clone had diversified. Single-cell sequencing revealed three distinct subclones, each with its own mutations. One carried the NRAS change. Another had lost a copy of chromosome seven, a grim marker of aggressive disease. The third, the most concerning, had acquired a TP53 mutation—R273H, a hotspot known to confer resistance to nearly every drug in their arsenal. The hematologist traced the timeline on the whiteboard. Day zero: B-ALL, KMT2A-rearranged, CD19-positive. Day twenty-eight: AML, same translocation, CD33-positive, NRAS-mutant. Day eighty-nine: AML with TP53 mutation, resistant to venetoclax. The leukemia wasn’t just switching identities. It was evolving in real time, its genetic code rewriting itself under the pressure of each new drug. The team had to move faster. They designed a monitoring protocol: peripheral blood flow cytometry every two weeks, next-generation sequencing every four. They knew the leukemia would adapt again. The question was whether they could outpace it. The KMT2A fusion gene, they realized, wasn’t just a driver. It was a chameleon, allowing the leukemia to shift between lymphoid and myeloid fates depending on the environment. Other leukemias—BCR-ABL1, ETV6-RUNX1—lacked this plasticity. But KMT2A was different. It kept the cells in a stem-like state, poised to change. Maria’s case forced a reckoning. The National Comprehensive Cancer Network updated its guidelines within months, now recommending monthly flow cytometry for KMT2A-rearranged leukemias and early consideration of combination therapies. 

Subscribe to No Known Cause. How real medicines were actually found.

 The American Society of Hematology presentation drew standing-room-only crowds, oncologists leaning in as the slides flashed: the same genetic lesion, two different diseases, one relentless enemy. In the hospital room, Maria’s hands trembled as she adjusted the IV line. The leukemia was no longer the same disease they had started treating. It had learned. It had fought back. And it wasn’t done yet. Maria’s blood had always been a battleground, but no one expected the war to shift sides. On the forty-seventh day after her first dose of blinatumomab, the leukemia that had clung to her marrow like a stubborn fog suddenly fractured. The blast count, which had hovered at thirty-two percent for weeks, plummeted to eight—then, just as abruptly, climbed back to twenty-one. The team’s microscopes revealed the truth: the original CD19-positive cells, once dominant, had vanished. In their place, a new army emerged, one that carried a different mutation, a different hunger. The NRAS gene, silent in her initial biopsies, now flared in forty-three percent of the remaining blasts, its mutated protein twisting the signals that told cells when to grow, when to die. They had anticipated resistance, but not this. Not a complete transformation, as if the leukemia had shed its skin overnight. The blinatumomab, designed to bind to CD19 like a key in a lock, had starved the first clone into submission—only to leave the door wide open for another. The team adjusted quickly, swapping the drug for trametinib, a small molecule that slipped into the NRAS pathway like a wrench in gears. Within three days, Maria’s fever broke. By the end of the week, her blast count dipped below fifteen percent. But the victory was fragile. The marrow aspirate showed whispers of a third clone, one that carried a TP53 mutation, lurking at the edges like a shadow waiting for its turn. They rotated the drugs like sentries on patrol: trametinib for the NRAS-driven cells, venetoclax to choke the BCL-2-dependent ones, decitabine to hammer the TP53 mutants before they could rise. The goal was never eradication. That was a fantasy. Instead, they aimed for balance, a standoff where no single clone could seize control. Maria’s blood became a ledger of numbers—blast counts, transfusion intervals, the milligrams of each drug she swallowed like clockwork. Some days, the leukemia retreated to five percent. Others, it surged back to eighteen. But it never broke free. Not entirely. She returned to her classroom, though her voice tired after forty minutes. The students didn’t know about the transfusions that kept her standing, or the way her fingers trembled when she wrote on the board. The team published their findings, calling it a proof of concept: cancer was not a single enemy, but a shifting alliance of rivals. And sometimes, the only way to survive was to let them fight each other. Subscribe to this channel for more documented cases.
